name: nilo
baseline: nginx 1.31.4 (C, custom handler module, -O3 -march=native) and h2o (C) in the HttpArena suite; Drogon, userver, hical, Cutelyst, agensio (C++) and mongoose, libreactorng, libioma (C) rows in the same tables
workload: HttpArena profiles on one 64-core machine: baseline (mixed GET/POST with query parsing, 4096 connections), pipelined, limited-conn, json-comp (gzip JSON), json-tls and HTTP/2 baseline; nilo is a Zig 0.17 HTTP server on zio fibers (io_uring, epoll, kqueue) with typed route functions.
claimed_speedup: README: '#2 of 79 on HTTP/1.1 and #1 of 22 on WebSocket, among untuned entries' on HttpArena. From the HttpArena JSON rows (ratios derived from page data): pipelined-4096 12,006,230 req/s vs nginx 4,037,345 (2.97x), h2o 4,938,603 (2.43x), Drogon 7,801,404 (1.54x); baseline-h2-256 7,267,874 vs nginx 3,414,750 (2.13x) and baseline-h2-1024 8,912,070 vs nginx 3,320,285 (2.68x); json-tls-4096 1,561,927 vs nginx 1,313,755 (1.19x), h2o 1,229,462 (1.27x), mongoose 1,102,964 (1.42x); json-comp-4096 611,376 vs userver 297,311 (2.06x), hical 261,955 (2.33x), Drogon 127,466 (4.80x); baseline-4096 3,076,550 vs Drogon 2,022,710 (1.52x) but nginx 3,284,513 (0.94x).
compiler_and_flags: nilo: zig build -Dtarget=... -Dcpu=... --release=fast (HttpArena frameworks/nilo/Dockerfile, alpine build, static binary). C/C++ rows: nginx 1.31.4 with a custom handler module built --with-cc-opt='-O3 -march=native -DNDEBUG'; h2o built with clang CMake Release -march=native -mtune=native (no LTO); mongoose gcc-14 -O3 -march=native -flto; Drogon CMake Release in the drogonframework/drogon image; userver CMake Release -march=native; libreactorng -O3 -march=native (HttpArena frameworks/<name>/Dockerfile).
hardware: HttpArena dedicated 64-core machine, one container per entry (README says '64-core dedicated hardware'; CPU model, RAM, NIC and kernel not stated)
tradeoffs: Experimental Zig 0.17 toolkit (HttpArena type 'experimental'); no HTTP/3 and no templates by its own statement; HTTP/2 and gRPC sit behind the -Dhttp2 build flag; small project with one main author.
caveats: It does not win everywhere: at baseline-4096 it is behind nginx (0.94x), h2o (0.84x), mongoose, hical, agensio and libreactorng (0.70x); at limited-conn-4096 it is behind nginx (2,301,647 vs 2,626,297); at pipelined-4096 libreactorng (C) reaches 43,424,448; at baseline-h2 h2o (16,106,978) and agensio (C++, 14,744,015) are well ahead; json-tls-4096 agensio 1,716,076 is ahead (0.91x). The nginx pipelined row (4.0M) is far below its non-pipelined rate, so the 2.97x pipelined ratio mostly reflects nginx's pipelining cost. The README's own numbers (1,401,412 req/s on four physical cores, p99 69 us) are first-party and the nilo comparison docs (docs/comparison.md) compare only against other managed-language servers, not C or C++; the C/C++ comparison here is the HttpArena rows. Results JSON files are undated and the suite is rerun by its maintainers; competitor rows are read from sibling JSON files in the same site/data/results directory; every entry is a minimal hand-written handler for the same endpoint contract (nginx runs a custom C handler module), and baseline-4096 mixes GET and POST with query parsing, not static files. CPU model is not stated, so not tier A.
found_via: Lead from the wave 14 web papers search ('more HttpArena entries to seed: nilo, edixoi, fib h2c'); WebFetch of github.com/MDA2AV/HttpArena/tree/main/site/data/results (file list) and /frameworks (meta.json, Dockerfile, README); per-entry JSON read via raw.githubusercontent.com and compared with every C/C++ row in the same directory
why_faster: Per the HttpArena entry description: fibers on zio over io_uring, one allocation per request, 4,669 bytes per idle connection, a wait parks the fiber rather than the thread; the README adds that nilo's own code is a small share of per-request CPU.

hardware: Intel(R) Xeon(R) CPU E5-1650 v3 @ 3.50GHz, 32G RAM (grpc_bench wiki page 2022-04-23; server limited to 1, 2 or 3 CPUs, client 9 CPUs)
tradeoffs: Rust async gRPC on tokio and hyper; the winning variant is single-threaded, so it cannot use more than one core per process; calling it from C++ needs a separate process.
caveats: Wins only when the server is limited to one CPU; C++ gRPC with its multi-threaded completion-queue server beats tonic from two CPUs up. The page is the 2022-04-23 run; the repo's Dockerfiles at HEAD (gcc 16.1, Rust 1.94, .NET 10, Go 1.26) are newer, so the numbers are not a reproduction of current code. The page states no compiler flags or library versions. The advantage appears only at the 1-CPU setting: with 2 and 3 CPUs cpp_grpc_mt leads (69,882 and 71,806 req/s) and the single-threaded C++ variants stay at about 26k, so the 1-CPU ratio compares against single-threaded C++ servers. Libgrpc++ comes from the distribution package, not a build tuned with the same flags. The tonic README makes no performance claim; the evidence is the third-party grpc_bench suite.

name: wut-server
baseline: nginx (C; own build with all optimization options, LTO, static OpenSSL, ngx_headers_more; 1 worker, 1024 worker connections, HTTP/2, TLS 1.3 only)
workload: wrk against a single endpoint that returns the caller's IP address: 10 s, 6 threads, 1000 connections (inferred from the output header), nginx on port 443 versus wut-server on port 11313 of the same host.
claimed_speedup: 38,110.60 requests/s (382,057 requests in 10 s) vs nginx 25,650.31 (257,322), about 49% more per the page (1.49x, derived from page data); transfer 3.27 MB/s vs 2.79 MB/s; max latency 279.57 ms vs 520.46 ms; nginx had connect 95 and read 17 socket errors.
compiler_and_flags: Rust build flags not stated; nginx build described above, version not stated.
hardware: Server: single-core AMD EPYC 7302P, 1 GB ECC RAM, 1 Gbit/s uplink; client: AMD Ryzen 5600, 32 GB ECC RAM, 250 Mbit/s uplink; OS not stated; network benchmark, not loopback.
tradeoffs: Single-purpose server that returns the caller's public IP over HTTP and HTTP/2; not a general web server.
caveats: First-party single run with no variance, no wrk command line and no versions. Average latency is higher for wut-server (45.00 ms vs 28.07 ms). The two servers listen on different ports and it is not stated whether wut-server terminates TLS on port 11313, so TLS work may differ; the run is over the network with a 250 Mbit/s client uplink and nginx shows socket errors, so the nginx side may be limited by the path rather than the server. The page compares only against nginx and the benchmark harness is not in the repo.

name: Pelikan Segcache (pelikan-segcache)
workload: Memcached-protocol cache server using the Segcache TTL-segmented storage and lockless worker threads; the README cites a joint evaluation with Intel ADQ and the Segcache blog for throughput scaling at 24 threads, and the NSDI'21 paper for memory efficiency.
claimed_speedup: README: 'the same architecture scaled to ~8x Memcached's throughput at 24 threads' (Segcache blog); metadata about 5 bytes per object (Memcached: 56); NSDI'21 paper: 40-90% less memory than Pelikan's own slab storage and 22-60% less than state-of-the-art research systems; a p999 under 5 ms SLO at 1M QPS per host with stacked instances.
tradeoffs: Rust workspace of cache services (segcache, rds, pingserver); Segcache is a TTL-centric design and the Memcached-like server is not a drop-in for every Memcached feature.
caveats: Throughput numbers sit only in the README summary: the Segcache blog (pelikan.io) and the peer-reviewed NSDI'21 paper it cites (usenix.org/conference/nsdi21/presentation/yang-juncheng) could not be opened from this environment (usenix.org did not resolve), so the 8x figure, thread counts, hardware and Memcached version are unverified; a verifier with paper access may raise this to B. The memory claims compare against Pelikan's own slab storage and research systems, not Memcached directly. A cache server rather than an HTTP server; included under serving.
found_via: Wave 14 search for Rust or Go servers claiming wins over C servers; github.com/pelikan-io/pelikan README
why_faster: Per the README: TTL-segmented storage amortizes metadata and locking by about 10,000x (segments instead of objects) and worker threads never wait on a peer (lockless queues).
